quote: Dance, when you’re broken open. / Dance, if you’ve torn the bandage off. / Dance in the middle of the fighting.
source: Rumi, The Essential Rumi, ch. 27, The Turn: Dance in Your Blood, p. 281 (trans. Coleman Barks with John Moyne, 1995)

evidence.where: Text extracted this run from a PDF of The Essential Rumi: the contents list chapter 27, The Turn: Dance in Your Blood, with this untitled piece last at p. 281; the poem is on the page; the References for chapter 27 give its Persian source; checked against Nicholson's Mathnawi, Book III
evidence.edition: The Essential Rumi, translations by Coleman Barks with John Moyne, HarperSanFrancisco, 1995
evidence.locator: ch. 27, The Turn: Dance in Your Blood, the untitled poem beginning Dance, when you're broken open, lines 1 to 3, p. 281

reason: The five line poem stands on p. 281 exactly as quoted, and the first three lines are taken whole, with the edition's lineation and capitals kept. Barks's own References for chapter 27 cite this piece as III, 95 to 97, that is Mathnawi Book III, and Nicholson's translation of those lines reads: Dance (only) where you break (mortify) yourself and (when you) tear away the cotton from the sore of lust. (Holy) men dance and wheel on the (spiritual) battle-field: they dance in their own blood. Broken open, the bandage torn off, the fighting and the blood are all there in order, so the line is Rumi's and the Persian place is fixed. Barks works from earlier English rather than from Persian and calls these versions, which is why the source names him as the translator whose wording this is.
